title: Build the six computable frontier artifacts, and split what is left from them
body:
Finishes every contract artifact this repository can honestly produce: **baselines, evaluation epoch, mission DAG, resource allocation, frontier checkpoint, final frontier state.**

One generator, because they are one computation read six ways — the checkpoint is the DAG plus the baselines, the allocation is the DAG filtered, the final state is all of it plus the completion law. Six generators would mean six reads of the same inputs and six chances to disagree about which head they describe.

## The baselines found something on their first run

| metric | recorded in `system-readiness.json` | live |
|---|---|---|
| files parsed | **871** | **2,190** |
| deterministic tests | **3,683** (3 failing) | **7,742** (0 failing) |
| mutations | **168** | **502** |

Every one of those was written down in good faith at a moment when it was true. What makes them dangerous is that they read exactly like a measurement taken now.

So a number's provenance travels with the number:

- `LIVE` was measured by the run that produced the artifact. `RECORDED` was copied from something somebody else wrote down, and carries its age.
- A recorded figure with **no timestamp is stale**, not fresh — currency can never be established for it at all, and defaulting it to fresh would make the least trustworthy figure in the file look like the best one.
- Where live and recorded disagree, **the disagreement is listed and neither is edited**. Overwriting the record destroys the evidence that it drifted; averaging them produces a number describing no tree.

## What the allocator refuses to do

It does not rank by expected value. No economic prior exists for any of this work, and inventing one would dress a guess as arithmetic. It allocates across missions actionable *now* and lists the rest with what they wait on — because a dependency is ours to clear and an external blocker is not, and conflating them turns a waiting list into a to-do list nobody can finish.

The epoch refuses to claim a trend: one epoch is `FIRST_EPOCH__NO_COMPARISON_POSSIBLE`, two are `CHANGE_MEASURED__TOO_FEW_EPOCHS_FOR_A_TREND`. A delta between two points is a difference, not a direction.

## The remainder, split

With those six written, **no absent contract artifact is computable any more**. `V7G009` now closes on computable work rather than total absence, and the eleven that remain move to `V7G010` as external:

| reason | count |
|---|---|
| `NEEDS_EXTERNAL_REALITY` | 5 |
| `NEEDS_REPEATED_OBSERVATION` | 4 |
| `NEEDS_A_RUNTIME_THAT_DOES_NOT_EXIST` | 1 |
| `NEEDS_ELAPSED_TIME` | 1 |

Same split already applied to the deployment gap, and the absence reasons it rests on were classified **before** any of these were built.

## Three things I had to fix rather than ship around

**`V7G005` was lying.** It counted commits ahead of main and reported "nothing stranded" while that very check sat uncommitted in the working tree. Uncommitted work is stranded in the most literal sense: it exists on one disk and nowhere else.

**A brittle assertion broke on an improvement.** `browser-runtime-pool` pinned the exact text `finally { await runtimeLease.release(); }` and went red when main improved the release to run under a bounded timeout — a strictly better version of the same guarantee. It now asserts the property, and I verified it still catches both real failure modes (release removed entirely; release moved out of `finally`). Red on main before this.

**My own test went stale.** It asserted some absences are ordinary work — true when written, false once I built them. Zero computable-now is the success state, but only if the remainder stays classified, so the assertions now defend *that*: no unclassified absence, and every remaining reason one that genuinely cannot be closed by writing code. Otherwise it would pass while real work hid behind a label.
